There's something weirdly mythical about the historical 4X and the dominance of a single series, Civilization, for 30 years. But Amplitude Studios has spent a decade preparing to rewrite that myth. Humankind is the result: a massive, history-spanning behemoth that's kept me on its hooks until sunrise a few times. But in trying to make its own Civilization, Amplitude may have sacrificed too much of what made its earlier games, Endless Legend in particular, such compelling weirdos.

This is not to say that Humankind doesn't have any bold ideas. It's clear that isn't the case as soon as you hop into a campaign. Normally you'd need to pick a civ, faction or race of nerdy dragons first, and then plonk down a city, but not here. Before picking a site for your first settlement, or even picking a culture, you must first explore the world as a nomadic, Neolithic tribe. During this phase you saunter around gathering food and other resources from nodes scattered all over the world, with breaks where you get to fight animals. Picking berries and beating up mammoths—a perfect Neolithic family day out.

I'm sure this all sounds quite relaxing—that's a trap. It's really a sprint, a particularly brutal one on the highest difficulty, where you're competing to get first dibs on the list of playable cultures and stake your claim on the most bountiful regions. Found a place with bronze and horses? Get an outpost on that as quickly as you can, and then get back to brawling with the wildlife.

Your little band of explorers will also grow, allowing you to break up the squad and send individual units or smaller groups far and wide. ## Stargazing

A bit like Civilization 6: Rise and Fall's Great Ages, Humankind only lets you move into a new era when you've hit enough milestones. Get seven stars for seven milestones and you'll be able to leap into the next era. Having these objectives is a fantastic motivator, and it's a good way to measure your progress against the competition. Unfortunately, the milestones are hardly inspiring. They're all arbitrary targets like 'research 60 techs' and 'defeat 20 military units', and the only thing that changes is the number. You'll be at turn 200 basically doing the same thing you were doing at turn 20. I think MMOs have broken me, though, because I do find the grind slightly reassuring.

![Image 25: A burgeoning city with a pyramid](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/o848CKzEqRkY3cZNL5fStB.jpg)[](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/o848CKzEqRkY3cZNL5fStB.jpg)

(Image credit: Sega)

While those stars are crucial, what you're really trying to get is the accompanying Fame payout—if you have the most when the game ends, victory is yours. So you might linger in an era you're free to leave, just so you can mop up a few more stars that you're close to getting. Watch out, though, because that Fame isn't going to save you if a more advanced empire decides to pick a fight. More Fame can be earned by erecting wonders, too, or by completing competitive deeds, like discovering natural wonders or landing on a new continent.

> It's simply the best 4X starting experience.

When it's time to hit the ancient era, it's only then that you get to pick your first culture. Each has a penchant for science, expansion, warfare and other specialities, giving you an active and passive ability shared by all the cultures with that affinity. You also get a unique building, unit and bonus, like Egypt's ability to generate more industrial power. The bonuses are usually big, game-changing numbers, and there's a significant difference if you pick, say, the industrious Egyptians over the expansionist Assyrians. These differences will determine, or at least inspire, your strategy, but mechanically they are a lot less distinct than any of the factions Amplitude has created previously. No numerical bonuses can really compare to the unique traits of Endless Legend's Necrophage, a ravenous insectoid swarm that can't make friends and just wants to eat everything, or Endless Space 2's Horatio, a faction filled with clones of the most narcissistic person in the galaxy.

Humankind's big trick is that you're not stuck with your chosen culture. At the start of every new era—there are six in total—you can optionally adopt a new era-appropriate culture while keeping the bonuses from your previous ones. Individually, the faction design seems conservative, but when you start mixing them up things start to get a lot more exciting. There are a million possible combinations, encouraging a lot of number crunching, theorycrafting and experimentation. You've also got lots of religious tenets, available to pick whenever your religion ranks up, and culture-wide civics decisions, both of which pile on even more bonuses. Overpowered builds are inevitable with this many combos, and I much prefer it to perfect balance.

![Image 26: Picking a new culture](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/dnoUFVqhNAwv7aUjfzLiPQ.jpg)[](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/dnoUFVqhNAwv7aUjfzLiPQ.jpg)

(Image credit: Sega)

A history of bugs

![Image 27: Humankind](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/hu7ZdvUaTpf5XsPY6wwqTQ.jpg)

(Image credit: Sega)

Humankind's performance remains buttery smooth even once you hit the endgame, but the review build still contained a few bugs. Some are known issues that should be fixed come launch, but I also encountered a few not on the list. Notifications sometimes displayed the wrong information, for instance, and the info box for neutral cities often displays the details of the wrong city. These cities can be assimilated by your empire if they trust you enough, and this bug makes it possible to assimilate cities you have no relationship with at all.

Watching my favourite numbers skyrocket brought me a lot of joy, but I can't say I got attached to any of my hybrid cultures. There's nothing to really get attached to—only the odd unique building or unit. And the individual cultures never stick around for very long, leaving behind only a bonus and the occasional relic—a pyramid here, an amphitheatre there—as their legacy. The AI leaders have personality traits, but I would never have been able to tell if the game didn't explicitly show me in the diplomacy screen. And it's much harder to nurture grudges when the civilisations keep changing.

Amplitude is so experienced in the art of weaving narrative twists into strategy games that its absence is Humankind's greatest surprise. I wouldn't expect something like Endless Legend's more scripted stories in a historical 4X, but Humankind doesn't really generate much emergent stuff either. There's this whole theme of multiculturalism that lies at the centre of Humankind that largely goes unexplored, beyond the obvious mechanical benefits. Even compared to Civilization, which has been known to let its hair down with things like rock band missionaries, it's utilitarian. You'll occasionally encounter some random events, but they're a half-hearted bunch and disconnected from the rest of the game.

It's telling that instead of your population's happiness or contentment being reflected, cities instead have a cold, mechanical stability meter. This, however, I'm OK with. I'm done with trying to keep people happy. All I want to do is build absolutely humongous cities, and Humankind is more than happy to be of service. These things consume everything and spread all over continents like a living factory, gobbling up all the resources and turning them into cash and guns. Feeding time is all the time.

![Image 31: The tech treee](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/BJfDw8mRrqAk8RZ6E9Y2AD.jpg)[](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/BJfDw8mRrqAk8RZ6E9Y2AD.jpg)

(Image credit: Sega)

By linking a region you've already claimed to an existing city, that city can then start expanding into the new region and harvesting its resources. Cities can even swallow up other cities, giving birth to a mega-city instantly. These big moves are pricey and destabilising, but with the economy's tendency to snowball, you can rack up a huge surplus pretty easily, and stability issues can be fixed by plonking down the appropriate district. There just isn't much—aside from your opponents—halting your expansion. When obstacles do appear, the solution is rarely to rein it in; you can always keep going.


## In search of war

I like the constant, consistent progression, and nobody likes being told they can't assimilate an empire today, but with more stringent limitations there'd also be more friction, more tension, and a more interesting strategy game. Thankfully, you can get to that game if you fiddle around with the settings a bit. See, the default settings will give you a game where nobody declares war, where you'll outpace everyone by multiple eras, and where you'll spend at least 100 turns just waiting around for something to happen. It put me right off. Just bumping it up a few notches to Empire difficulty (there are two more beyond that) makes a world of difference, especially if you shrink the map down to make the fight over territory a lot nastier.

When I turned the difficulty up the first time, the Neolithic tribes were going at it even before they'd invented the concept of war, and by the second era everyone was getting stuck into some much more serious scuffles. The need for troops massively slowed down the development of my cities and my economy, and while cheesy builds can still throw it all into (welcome) disarray, the AI can at least give you a proper fight when you let it off the leash. I'm actually losing a war terribly in my current campaign. It's great!

![Image 32: Making treaties in the diplomacy menu](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/wSVLi6MhjrFsMvGVa8DmyB.jpg)[](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/wSVLi6MhjrFsMvGVa8DmyB.jpg)

(Image credit: Sega)

There's just one problem: I don't really like fighting. The threat of combat is a necessary evil to shake up a game that can be a little dull without it. Fights play out in a tactical map within the campaign map, with each unit in your squad getting a chance to bloody the enemy's nose. It's a lot like Endless Legend's combat system, but not as good. Units can move, use one basic attack and die—that's their three skills. Terrain is the main enemy, and with more elaborate topography than Endless Legend, there's less room to work with. It's more fiddly than tactical, and I'm still confused about how I'm meant to lay siege to small islands when, as the game kept reminding me, "you can't besiege a city with an army at sea". Thanks.

> The threat of combat is a necessary evil to shake up a game that can be a little dull without it.

If units had more utility, it would be greatly improved, and things do pick up a bit once you start getting close to the end of the tech tree, but I always hit that auto-resolve button the instant I see I have even a slight advantage. At least it's an option. And with the actual fights out of the way, there's a lot to war worth recommending—it really spices up a relationship that's on the rocks.

Even with more enthusiastic opponents, the momentum falters in the endgame as Humankind runs out of new tricks. It gets familiar late additions like the space race, nukes and pollution, but all of them are disappointingly perfunctory. I sped to the end of the very traditional tech tree in my first game, and acquiring all of humanity's knowledge only left me hollow. Perhaps there's a valuable lesson in there, but I'd rather have more neat things to do with fancy technology. There are only so many times the numbers can grow before you crave something a bit more substantial.

![Image 33: A large, modern city](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/coS6hFDS8uMucHH5cbbNFC.jpg)[](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/coS6hFDS8uMucHH5cbbNFC.jpg)

(Image credit: Sega)

Old World serves as an interesting comparison. Like Humankind, Civ's influence is everywhere, but while that gave Old World a starting point, where it ended up was a lot more unusual. It found a new place to focus on—people—and all sorts of surprising crises and obstacles as a result, like being murdered by your nephew. While Humankind has reconsidered and reconfigured Civ's features, it's been more reserved. Being able to adopt new cultures and nurture continent-sized cities is certainly novel, but it isn't transformative. It could probably do with being 20% weirder, I reckon. I've done the maths. And I've had lots of practice, given Humankind's aforementioned love of big numbers.

*   [**Humankind guide**](https://www.pcgamer.com/humankind-guide-tips/)**:** How to get started

The End Turn button still beckons, however, and Memphis needs more oil for its battleships. I also need to try out a lethal militant build I've been considering, in the hopes of quickly throwing the world into an apocalyptic war. Humankind has still spawned some great ideas that I'm not done with, and can't wait to see imitated and iterated. But now that Amplitude has made its Civilization, I really hope it goes back to making Alpha Centauris.

There's something weirdly mythical about the historical 4X and the dominance of a single series, Civilization, for 30 years. But Amplitude Studios has spent a decade preparing to rewrite that myth. Humankind is the result: a massive, history-spanning behemoth that's kept me on its hooks until sunrise a few times. But in trying to make its own Civilization, Amplitude may have sacrificed too much of what made its earlier games, Endless Legend in particular, such compelling weirdos.

This is not to say that Humankind doesn't have any bold ideas. It's clear that isn't the case as soon as you hop into a campaign. Normally you'd need to pick a civ, faction or race of nerdy dragons first, and then plonk down a city, but not here. Before picking a site for your first settlement, or even picking a culture, you must first explore the world as a nomadic, Neolithic tribe. During this phase you saunter around gathering food and other resources from nodes scattered all over the world, with breaks where you get to fight animals. Picking berries and beating up mammoths—a perfect Neolithic family day out.

I'm sure this all sounds quite relaxing—that's a trap. It's really a sprint, a particularly brutal one on the highest difficulty, where you're competing to get first dibs on the list of playable cultures and stake your claim on the most bountiful regions. Found a place with bronze and horses? Get an outpost on that as quickly as you can, and then get back to brawling with the wildlife.

## Stargazing

A bit like Civilization 6: Rise and Fall's Great Ages, Humankind only lets you move into a new era when you've hit enough milestones. Get seven stars for seven milestones and you'll be able to leap into the next era. Having these objectives is a fantastic motivator, and it's a good way to measure your progress against the competition. Unfortunately, the milestones are hardly inspiring. They're all arbitrary targets like 'research 60 techs' and 'defeat 20 military units', and the only thing that changes is the number. You'll be at turn 200 basically doing the same thing you were doing at turn 20. I think MMOs have broken me, though, because I do find the grind slightly reassuring.

![Image 25: A burgeoning city with a pyramid](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/o848CKzEqRkY3cZNL5fStB.jpg)[](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/o848CKzEqRkY3cZNL5fStB.jpg)

(Image credit: Sega)

While those stars are crucial, what you're really trying to get is the accompanying Fame payout—if you have the most when the game ends, victory is yours. So you might linger in an era you're free to leave, just so you can mop up a few more stars that you're close to getting. Watch out, though, because that Fame isn't going to save you if a more advanced empire decides to pick a fight. More Fame can be earned by erecting wonders, too, or by completing competitive deeds, like discovering natural wonders or landing on a new continent.

> It's simply the best 4X starting experience.

When it's time to hit the ancient era, it's only then that you get to pick your first culture. Each has a penchant for science, expansion, warfare and other specialities, giving you an active and passive ability shared by all the cultures with that affinity. You also get a unique building, unit and bonus, like Egypt's ability to generate more industrial power. The bonuses are usually big, game-changing numbers, and there's a significant difference if you pick, say, the industrious Egyptians over the expansionist Assyrians. These differences will determine, or at least inspire, your strategy, but mechanically they are a lot less distinct than any of the factions Amplitude has created previously. No numerical bonuses can really compare to the unique traits of Endless Legend's Necrophage, a ravenous insectoid swarm that can't make friends and just wants to eat everything, or Endless Space 2's Horatio, a faction filled with clones of the most narcissistic person in the galaxy.

Humankind's big trick is that you're not stuck with your chosen culture. At the start of every new era—there are six in total—you can optionally adopt a new era-appropriate culture while keeping the bonuses from your previous ones. Individually, the faction design seems conservative, but when you start mixing them up things start to get a lot more exciting. There are a million possible combinations, encouraging a lot of number crunching, theorycrafting and experimentation. You've also got lots of religious tenets, available to pick whenever your religion ranks up, and culture-wide civics decisions, both of which pile on even more bonuses. Overpowered builds are inevitable with this many combos, and I much prefer it to perfect balance.

![Image 26: Picking a new culture](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/dnoUFVqhNAwv7aUjfzLiPQ.jpg)[](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/dnoUFVqhNAwv7aUjfzLiPQ.jpg)

(Image credit: Sega)

A history of bugs

![Image 27: Humankind](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/hu7ZdvUaTpf5XsPY6wwqTQ.jpg)

(Image credit: Sega)

Humankind's performance remains buttery smooth even once you hit the endgame, but the review build still contained a few bugs. Some are known issues that should be fixed come launch, but I also encountered a few not on the list. Notifications sometimes displayed the wrong information, for instance, and the info box for neutral cities often displays the details of the wrong city. These cities can be assimilated by your empire if they trust you enough, and this bug makes it possible to assimilate cities you have no relationship with at all.

Watching my favourite numbers skyrocket brought me a lot of joy, but I can't say I got attached to any of my hybrid cultures. There's nothing to really get attached to—only the odd unique building or unit. And the individual cultures never stick around for very long, leaving behind only a bonus and the occasional relic—a pyramid here, an amphitheatre there—as their legacy. The AI leaders have personality traits, but I would never have been able to tell if the game didn't explicitly show me in the diplomacy screen. And it's much harder to nurture grudges when the civilisations keep changing.

Amplitude is so experienced in the art of weaving narrative twists into strategy games that its absence is Humankind's greatest surprise. I wouldn't expect something like Endless Legend's more scripted stories in a historical 4X, but Humankind doesn't really generate much emergent stuff either. There's this whole theme of multiculturalism that lies at the centre of Humankind that largely goes unexplored, beyond the obvious mechanical benefits. Even compared to Civilization, which has been known to let its hair down with things like rock band missionaries, it's utilitarian. You'll occasionally encounter some random events, but they're a half-hearted bunch and disconnected from the rest of the game.

It's telling that instead of your population's happiness or contentment being reflected, cities instead have a cold, mechanical stability meter. This, however, I'm OK with. I'm done with trying to keep people happy. All I want to do is build absolutely humongous cities, and Humankind is more than happy to be of service. These things consume everything and spread all over continents like a living factory, gobbling up all the resources and turning them into cash and guns. Feeding time is all the time.

![Image 31: The tech treee](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/BJfDw8mRrqAk8RZ6E9Y2AD.jpg)[](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/BJfDw8mRrqAk8RZ6E9Y2AD.jpg)

(Image credit: Sega)

By linking a region you've already claimed to an existing city, that city can then start expanding into the new region and harvesting its resources. Cities can even swallow up other cities, giving birth to a mega-city instantly. These big moves are pricey and destabilising, but with the economy's tendency to snowball, you can rack up a huge surplus pretty easily, and stability issues can be fixed by plonking down the appropriate district. There just isn't much—aside from your opponents—halting your expansion. When obstacles do appear, the solution is rarely to rein it in; you can always keep going.


## In search of war

I like the constant, consistent progression, and nobody likes being told they can't assimilate an empire today, but with more stringent limitations there'd also be more friction, more tension, and a more interesting strategy game. Thankfully, you can get to that game if you fiddle around with the settings a bit. See, the default settings will give you a game where nobody declares war, where you'll outpace everyone by multiple eras, and where you'll spend at least 100 turns just waiting around for something to happen. It put me right off. Just bumping it up a few notches to Empire difficulty (there are two more beyond that) makes a world of difference, especially if you shrink the map down to make the fight over territory a lot nastier.

When I turned the difficulty up the first time, the Neolithic tribes were going at it even before they'd invented the concept of war, and by the second era everyone was getting stuck into some much more serious scuffles. The need for troops massively slowed down the development of my cities and my economy, and while cheesy builds can still throw it all into (welcome) disarray, the AI can at least give you a proper fight when you let it off the leash. I'm actually losing a war terribly in my current campaign. It's great!

![Image 32: Making treaties in the diplomacy menu](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/wSVLi6MhjrFsMvGVa8DmyB.jpg)[](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/wSVLi6MhjrFsMvGVa8DmyB.jpg)

(Image credit: Sega)

There's just one problem: I don't really like fighting. The threat of combat is a necessary evil to shake up a game that can be a little dull without it. Fights play out in a tactical map within the campaign map, with each unit in your squad getting a chance to bloody the enemy's nose. It's a lot like Endless Legend's combat system, but not as good. Units can move, use one basic attack and die—that's their three skills. Terrain is the main enemy, and with more elaborate topography than Endless Legend, there's less room to work with. It's more fiddly than tactical, and I'm still confused about how I'm meant to lay siege to small islands when, as the game kept reminding me, "you can't besiege a city with an army at sea". Thanks.

> The threat of combat is a necessary evil to shake up a game that can be a little dull without it.

If units had more utility, it would be greatly improved, and things do pick up a bit once you start getting close to the end of the tech tree, but I always hit that auto-resolve button the instant I see I have even a slight advantage. At least it's an option. And with the actual fights out of the way, there's a lot to war worth recommending—it really spices up a relationship that's on the rocks.

Even with more enthusiastic opponents, the momentum falters in the endgame as Humankind runs out of new tricks. It gets familiar late additions like the space race, nukes and pollution, but all of them are disappointingly perfunctory. I sped to the end of the very traditional tech tree in my first game, and acquiring all of humanity's knowledge only left me hollow. Perhaps there's a valuable lesson in there, but I'd rather have more neat things to do with fancy technology. There are only so many times the numbers can grow before you crave something a bit more substantial.

![Image 33: A large, modern city](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/coS6hFDS8uMucHH5cbbNFC.jpg)[](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/coS6hFDS8uMucHH5cbbNFC.jpg)

(Image credit: Sega)

Old World serves as an interesting comparison. Like Humankind, Civ's influence is everywhere, but while that gave Old World a starting point, where it ended up was a lot more unusual. It found a new place to focus on—people—and all sorts of surprising crises and obstacles as a result, like being murdered by your nephew. While Humankind has reconsidered and reconfigured Civ's features, it's been more reserved. Being able to adopt new cultures and nurture continent-sized cities is certainly novel, but it isn't transformative. It could probably do with being 20% weirder, I reckon. I've done the maths. And I've had lots of practice, given Humankind's aforementioned love of big numbers.

*   [**Humankind guide**](https://www.pcgamer.com/humankind-guide-tips/)**:** How to get started

The End Turn button still beckons, however, and Memphis needs more oil for its battleships. I also need to try out a lethal militant build I've been considering, in the hopes of quickly throwing the world into an apocalyptic war. Humankind has still spawned some great ideas that I'm not done with, and can't wait to see imitated and iterated. But now that Amplitude has made its Civilization, I really hope it goes back to making Alpha Centauris.

Several features, specifically those related to online functionality, no longer work in Shadow of Mordor.

WB Games cited “changes with our network” as the reason for Shadow of Mordor’s servers to have gone offline. As a result, several online features, like Nemesis Forge and Vendetta missions, are no longer available on PC (via Steam), PlayStation 4, and Xbox One.

 Advertisement 

Players familiar with the game’s sequel, 2017’s [Middle-earth: Shadow of War](https://www.gamespot.com/games/middle-earth-shadow-of-war/), may recall the Nemesis Forge. A featured added to Shadow of Mordor shortly before Shadow of War launched, Nemesis Forge allowed players to import their most-hated nemesis and most-loyal ally from Mordor into War. This feature is offline now that the servers have shut down.

The same is true for Vendetta missions, tasks that saw players track down and beat powerful orcs that have killed other players in their own games. This feature is also offline now.

Other features that not are no longer functional in Shadow of Mordor include leaderboards and the WBPlay platform. While some features go offline, a few achievements can still be unlocked, including “Lord of the Ring,” “Rapid in Blood,” and “The Hunt is My Mistress.” Furthermore, because they were connected to the WBPlay platform and that’s now offline, the Epic runes “Gravewalker” and “Orc Hunter” are automatically awarded to all players.

Shadow of Mordor is a six-year-old game now, originally launching in September 2014 for PC, PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, Xbox 360, and Xbox One. The sequel, Shadow of War, was met with criticism over its use of microtransactions, which were later [cut from the game entirely](https://www.gamespot.com/articles/middle-earth-shadow-of-wars-microtransaction-marke/1100-6460470/).

In other Lord of the Rings new, the long-running Lord of the Rings Online MMO from publisher Daybreak Game Company may be [preparing to launch on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S](https://www.gamespot.com/articles/lord-of-the-rings-online-is-coming-to-ps5-and-xbox-series-x-it-seems/1100-6485202/).

WB Games cited “changes with our network” as the reason for Shadow of Mordor’s servers to have gone offline. As a result, several online features, like Nemesis Forge and Vendetta missions, are no longer available on PC (via Steam), PlayStation 4, and Xbox One.

 Advertisement 

Players familiar with the game’s sequel, 2017’s [Middle-earth: Shadow of War](https://www.gamespot.com/games/middle-earth-shadow-of-war/), may recall the Nemesis Forge. A featured added to Shadow of Mordor shortly before Shadow of War launched, Nemesis Forge allowed players to import their most-hated nemesis and most-loyal ally from Mordor into War. This feature is offline now that the servers have shut down.

The same is true for Vendetta missions, tasks that saw players track down and beat powerful orcs that have killed other players in their own games. This feature is also offline now.

Other features that not are no longer functional in Shadow of Mordor include leaderboards and the WBPlay platform. While some features go offline, a few achievements can still be unlocked, including “Lord of the Ring,” “Rapid in Blood,” and “The Hunt is My Mistress.” Furthermore, because they were connected to the WBPlay platform and that’s now offline, the Epic runes “Gravewalker” and “Orc Hunter” are automatically awarded to all players.

Shadow of Mordor is a six-year-old game now, originally launching in September 2014 for PC, PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, Xbox 360, and Xbox One. The sequel, Shadow of War, was met with criticism over its use of microtransactions, which were later [cut from the game entirely](https://www.gamespot.com/articles/middle-earth-shadow-of-wars-microtransaction-marke/1100-6460470/).

In other Lord of the Rings new, the long-running Lord of the Rings Online MMO from publisher Daybreak Game Company may be [preparing to launch on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S](https://www.gamespot.com/articles/lord-of-the-rings-online-is-coming-to-ps5-and-xbox-series-x-it-seems/1100-6485202/).

_**Humankind**_ is a [turn-based strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn-based_strategy "Turn-based strategy")[4X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4X "4X") video game by [Amplitude Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios "Amplitude Studios") and published by [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega"). The game was released for [Microsoft Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") and [Stadia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Stadia "Google Stadia") in August 2021, for [macOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacOS "MacOS") in November 2021, and for PlayStation and Xbox consoles in August 2023. It received generally favorable reviews.

## Gameplay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Humankind_(video_game)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Gameplay")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/91/Humankind_game_screenshot.jpg/250px-Humankind_game_screenshot.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Humankind_game_screenshot.jpg)

Military units in _Humankind_ can take advantage of terrain.

_Humankind_ is a [4X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4X "4X") game comparable to the _[Civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilization\_(series) "Civilization (series)")_ series. Players lead their civilization across six major [eras of human civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodization "Periodization"), starting from the [nomadic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomad "Nomad") age, directing how the civilization should expand, developing cities, controlling military and other types of units as they interact with other civilizations on the virtual planet, randomly generated at the start of a new game. A distinguishing feature of _Humankind_ is that within each of the eras, the player selects one of ten civilization types based on historical societies; this selection offers both bonuses and penalties to how the player can build out the civilization. Because a player can select different civilizations as templates to build upon, there exist potentially one million different civilization patterns that a player can ultimately develop.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-rpg_announce-2)

Building out cities follows a similar model from Amplitude's _[Endless Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endless\_Legend "Endless Legend")_ game, a continent in _Humankind_ will have multiple territories on it, and the player will only be able to build one city in that territory. Over time, they can expand that city, adding farms and other outlying resources as well as more dense urban areas closer to the city center. This allows the creation of large metropolises within each territory.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-rpg_announce-2) Players may also need to engage in combat with enemy forces. When this occurs, the game uses a [tactical role-playing game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tactical_role-playing_game "Tactical role-playing game") approach for detailed resolution of these battles, giving the player a chance to take advantage of terrain and special abilities of their units.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-rpg_announce-2) Within these skirmishes, battles can only last for three combat turns before the game returns to the overworld, so that drawn-out wars can occur across multiple years at the overworld scale.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-ign_preview-3)

During the game, the players gain resources for their civilization, similar to _Endless Legend_, which includes food, industry, gold, science, and influence; each of these can be spent to speed up production, advance technology, or as trade goods with other cultures. _Humankind_ also includes Fame, which is earned by feats within the game, for example, accumulating influence or gold, destroying units, being the first civilization to discover certain technologies, or build [world wonders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonders_of_the_World "Wonders of the World"). Fame is a persistent measure of a civilization's relative success compared to other civilizations, and can impact later decisions in the game. Unlike games like _Civilization_ where there can be multiple victory conditions, victory in _Humankind_ is based solely on the Fame score after a pre-determined number of turns,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-ign_preview-3) or other events that trigger end-game. _Humankind_ will include certain persons and events based on historical records that the player will interact with.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-4)

## Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Humankind_(video_game)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Development")]

[Amplitude Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios "Amplitude Studios") has had a history of prior 4X games based on its _Endless_[science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") setting, including _[Endless Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endless\_Space "Endless Space")_ and _[Endless Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endless\_Legend "Endless Legend")_. The studio considers _Humankind_ to be their [magnum opus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masterpiece "Masterpiece") of their previous titles,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-rpg_announce-2) and something that they have wanted to produce from the start, with their recent acquisition by [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega") helping to make _Humankind_ possible.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-ign_preview-3)

_Humankind_ had been teased by Sega earlier in 2019, with the game formally announced during the August 2019 [Gamescom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamescom "Gamescom").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-rpg_announce-2) The game had an exclusive 7-day demo available on [Stadia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Stadia "Google Stadia"), starting on October 21, 2020.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-6)

Amplitude held periods of open beta testing across late 2020 and early 2021, called "OpenDev" phases, giving players the opportunity to try limited scenarios and provide feedback for improving the game.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-7)

While the game was planned for an April 2021 release, Amplitude pushed the release into August 2021 to facilitate final polishing of the game.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-8) During this time, Amplitude announced they would not include [Denuvo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denuvo "Denuvo") digital rights management software in the game. While they had intended to use Denuvo to help protect their game, data collected during the OpenDev phases found that Denuvo negatively impacted the performance of the game, and they opted to remove the software.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-9)

An expansion, titled _Together We Rule_, was released on November 9, 2022.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-10)

Humankind was scheduled to release on [PlayStation 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_4 "PlayStation 4"), [PlayStation 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_5 "PlayStation 5"), [Xbox One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_One "Xbox One"), and [Xbox Series X/S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_Series_X/S "Xbox Series X/S") in November 2022 but was delayed indefinitely due to “unique porting challenges”, eventually releasing in August 2023.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-12)

_[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")_ writer Leana Hafner felt the game fell short of its potential, stating "Humankind is an interesting but fairly safe riff on historical 4X that doesn't always rise to meet its potential."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-IGN-15)_[PC Gamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PC\_Gamer "PC Gamer")_ writer Fraser Brown enjoyed the process of watching civilizations grow, but felt that the gameplay was too numbers-focused and lacked the personality and narrative uniqueness of Amplitude's earlier works.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-PC_Gamer-16) Writing for _[Rock Paper Shotgun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock\_Paper\_Shotgun "Rock Paper Shotgun")_, Nate Crowley compared the game favorably to the [Civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilization_(series) "Civilization (series)") series, but felt the game didn't allow for diplomatic or military playstyles, writing "In more games than not, I find I'm devoting the bare minimum effort to military action and diplomacy, since land development almost always represents a more efficient way of getting what I want".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-18)

_[Kotaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kotaku "Kotaku")_ writer Luke Plunkett spoke positively of the player's ability to switch cultures mid-game, writing "I hate being locked into a certain playstyle before I've ever seen the map or my opponents in a game like this, so getting the chance to reroll my empire constantly throughout the game is probably _Humankind's_ smartest new idea".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-19)_[Eurogamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurogamer "Eurogamer")_ writer Chris Tapsell wrote positively of the game's combat, but felt that the game's mechanics sacrificed fun for authenticity.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-Eurogamer_review-20)

### Awards and accolades

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Humankind_(video_game)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Awards and accolades")]

_Humankind_ was nominated for Best Sim/Strategy Game at [The Game Awards 2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Game_Awards_2021 "The Game Awards 2021").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-21)

### Sales

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Humankind_(video_game)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Sales")]

_Humankind_ was the fourth best-selling video game in August 2021 in the US.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-22)

_**Humankind**_ is a [turn-based strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn-based_strategy "Turn-based strategy")[4X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4X "4X") video game by [Amplitude Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios "Amplitude Studios") and published by [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega"). The game was released for [Microsoft Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") and [Stadia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Stadia "Google Stadia") in August 2021, for [macOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacOS "MacOS") in November 2021, and for PlayStation and Xbox consoles in August 2023. It received generally favorable reviews.

## Gameplay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Humankind_(video_game)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Gameplay")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/91/Humankind_game_screenshot.jpg/250px-Humankind_game_screenshot.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Humankind_game_screenshot.jpg)

Military units in _Humankind_ can take advantage of terrain.

_Humankind_ is a [4X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4X "4X") game comparable to the _[Civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilization\_(series) "Civilization (series)")_ series. Players lead their civilization across six major [eras of human civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodization "Periodization"), starting from the [nomadic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomad "Nomad") age, directing how the civilization should expand, developing cities, controlling military and other types of units as they interact with other civilizations on the virtual planet, randomly generated at the start of a new game. A distinguishing feature of _Humankind_ is that within each of the eras, the player selects one of ten civilization types based on historical societies; this selection offers both bonuses and penalties to how the player can build out the civilization. Because a player can select different civilizations as templates to build upon, there exist potentially one million different civilization patterns that a player can ultimately develop.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-rpg_announce-2)

Building out cities follows a similar model from Amplitude's _[Endless Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endless\_Legend "Endless Legend")_ game, a continent in _Humankind_ will have multiple territories on it, and the player will only be able to build one city in that territory. Over time, they can expand that city, adding farms and other outlying resources as well as more dense urban areas closer to the city center. This allows the creation of large metropolises within each territory.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-rpg_announce-2) Players may also need to engage in combat with enemy forces. When this occurs, the game uses a [tactical role-playing game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tactical_role-playing_game "Tactical role-playing game") approach for detailed resolution of these battles, giving the player a chance to take advantage of terrain and special abilities of their units.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-rpg_announce-2) Within these skirmishes, battles can only last for three combat turns before the game returns to the overworld, so that drawn-out wars can occur across multiple years at the overworld scale.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-ign_preview-3)

During the game, the players gain resources for their civilization, similar to _Endless Legend_, which includes food, industry, gold, science, and influence; each of these can be spent to speed up production, advance technology, or as trade goods with other cultures. _Humankind_ also includes Fame, which is earned by feats within the game, for example, accumulating influence or gold, destroying units, being the first civilization to discover certain technologies, or build [world wonders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonders_of_the_World "Wonders of the World"). Fame is a persistent measure of a civilization's relative success compared to other civilizations, and can impact later decisions in the game. Unlike games like _Civilization_ where there can be multiple victory conditions, victory in _Humankind_ is based solely on the Fame score after a pre-determined number of turns,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-ign_preview-3) or other events that trigger end-game. _Humankind_ will include certain persons and events based on historical records that the player will interact with.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-4)

## Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Humankind_(video_game)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Development")]

[Amplitude Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios "Amplitude Studios") has had a history of prior 4X games based on its _Endless_[science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction "Science fiction") setting, including _[Endless Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endless\_Space "Endless Space")_ and _[Endless Legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endless\_Legend "Endless Legend")_. The studio considers _Humankind_ to be their [magnum opus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masterpiece "Masterpiece") of their previous titles,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-rpg_announce-2) and something that they have wanted to produce from the start, with their recent acquisition by [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega") helping to make _Humankind_ possible.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-ign_preview-3)

_Humankind_ had been teased by Sega earlier in 2019, with the game formally announced during the August 2019 [Gamescom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamescom "Gamescom").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-rpg_announce-2) The game had an exclusive 7-day demo available on [Stadia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Stadia "Google Stadia"), starting on October 21, 2020.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-6)

Amplitude held periods of open beta testing across late 2020 and early 2021, called "OpenDev" phases, giving players the opportunity to try limited scenarios and provide feedback for improving the game.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-7)

While the game was planned for an April 2021 release, Amplitude pushed the release into August 2021 to facilitate final polishing of the game.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-8) During this time, Amplitude announced they would not include [Denuvo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denuvo "Denuvo") digital rights management software in the game. While they had intended to use Denuvo to help protect their game, data collected during the OpenDev phases found that Denuvo negatively impacted the performance of the game, and they opted to remove the software.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-9)

An expansion, titled _Together We Rule_, was released on November 9, 2022.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-10)

Humankind was scheduled to release on [PlayStation 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_4 "PlayStation 4"), [PlayStation 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_5 "PlayStation 5"), [Xbox One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_One "Xbox One"), and [Xbox Series X/S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_Series_X/S "Xbox Series X/S") in November 2022 but was delayed indefinitely due to “unique porting challenges”, eventually releasing in August 2023.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-12)

_Humankind_ received "generally favorable reviews", according to [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") platform [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-MC-13)

_[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")_ writer Leana Hafner felt the game fell short of its potential, stating "Humankind is an interesting but fairly safe riff on historical 4X that doesn't always rise to meet its potential."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-IGN-15)_[PC Gamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PC\_Gamer "PC Gamer")_ writer Fraser Brown enjoyed the process of watching civilizations grow, but felt that the gameplay was too numbers-focused and lacked the personality and narrative uniqueness of Amplitude's earlier works.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-PC_Gamer-16) Writing for _[Rock Paper Shotgun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock\_Paper\_Shotgun "Rock Paper Shotgun")_, Nate Crowley compared the game favorably to the [Civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilization_(series) "Civilization (series)") series, but felt the game didn't allow for diplomatic or military playstyles, writing "In more games than not, I find I'm devoting the bare minimum effort to military action and diplomacy, since land development almost always represents a more efficient way of getting what I want".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-18)

_[Kotaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kotaku "Kotaku")_ writer Luke Plunkett spoke positively of the player's ability to switch cultures mid-game, writing "I hate being locked into a certain playstyle before I've ever seen the map or my opponents in a game like this, so getting the chance to reroll my empire constantly throughout the game is probably _Humankind's_ smartest new idea".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-19)_[Eurogamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurogamer "Eurogamer")_ writer Chris Tapsell wrote positively of the game's combat, but felt that the game's mechanics sacrificed fun for authenticity.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humankind_(video_game)#cite_note-Eurogamer_review-20)

Where your donation goes

 Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](https://wikimediafoundation.org/annualreports/current/) for more information about our financial health. 

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

12% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 
Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

11% General and Administrative Expenses 
Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

**Amplitude Studios SASU** is a French [video game developer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_developer "Video game developer") based in Paris. The studio was founded in January 2011 by former [Ubisoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubisoft "Ubisoft") employees Romain de Waubert de Genlis and Mathieu Girard. [Sega Sammy Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Sammy_Holdings "Sega Sammy Holdings") acquired it in June 2016 and became part of [Sega Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Europe "Sega Europe") until it became independent again in 2024.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-2)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amplitude_Studios&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Amplitude Studios focuses primarily on the development of titles for the [personal computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_computer "Personal computer") (PC), and uses [Steam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_(service) "Steam (service)")'s [Early Access programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_Early_Access "Steam Early Access"), as well as Games2Gether, a crowd-sourcing and voting platform developed by Amplitude Studios, for players to suggest and vote on design choices that should be taken into games from Amplitude Studios, to create a player-centered experience.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-6)

In July 2016, [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega") announced that it had acquired Amplitude Studios in order to expand its reach on the [PC gaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PC_gaming "PC gaming") market.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-7) Founders Girard and de Waubert de Genlis stated that they agreed on the deal as they saw the opportunity to work alongside other Sega-owned studios, such as [Creative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Assembly "Creative Assembly") and [Relic Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relic_Entertainment "Relic Entertainment").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-8)

Girard eventually left Amplitude in 2018 after the release of Endless Space 2 to start his own company "Tactical Adventures",[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-9) and would later go on to release [Solasta: Crown of the Magister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solasta:_Crown_of_the_Magister "Solasta: Crown of the Magister").

Amplitude Studios bought itself out from Sega and became an independent company in November 2024. Sega would continue to support Amplitude's current and planned near-term games during a transition period.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-10)

Where your donation goes

 Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](https://wikimediafoundation.org/annualreports/current/) for more information about our financial health. 

45% Investment in Technology 
Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

32% Support for Volunteers 
The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

12% Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 
Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

11% General and Administrative Expenses 
Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

**Amplitude Studios SASU** is a French [video game developer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_developer "Video game developer") based in Paris. The studio was founded in January 2011 by former [Ubisoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubisoft "Ubisoft") employees Romain de Waubert de Genlis and Mathieu Girard. [Sega Sammy Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Sammy_Holdings "Sega Sammy Holdings") acquired it in June 2016 and became part of [Sega Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Europe "Sega Europe") until it became independent again in 2024.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-2)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amplitude_Studios&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Amplitude Studios focuses primarily on the development of titles for the [personal computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_computer "Personal computer") (PC), and uses [Steam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_(service) "Steam (service)")'s [Early Access programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_Early_Access "Steam Early Access"), as well as Games2Gether, a crowd-sourcing and voting platform developed by Amplitude Studios, for players to suggest and vote on design choices that should be taken into games from Amplitude Studios, to create a player-centered experience.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-6)

In July 2016, [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega") announced that it had acquired Amplitude Studios in order to expand its reach on the [PC gaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PC_gaming "PC gaming") market.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-7) Founders Girard and de Waubert de Genlis stated that they agreed on the deal as they saw the opportunity to work alongside other Sega-owned studios, such as [Creative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Assembly "Creative Assembly") and [Relic Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relic_Entertainment "Relic Entertainment").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-8)

Girard eventually left Amplitude in 2018 after the release of Endless Space 2 to start his own company "Tactical Adventures",[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-9) and would later go on to release [Solasta: Crown of the Magister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solasta:_Crown_of_the_Magister "Solasta: Crown of the Magister").

Amplitude Studios bought itself out from Sega and became an independent company in November 2024. Sega would continue to support Amplitude's current and planned near-term games during a transition period.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplitude_Studios#cite_note-10)

_**Total War: Three Kingdoms**_ is a [turn-based strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn-based_strategy "Turn-based strategy")[real-time tactics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real-time_tactics "Real-time tactics")[video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game "Video game") developed by [Creative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Assembly "Creative Assembly") and published by [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega"). As the 12th mainline entry (the 13th entry) in the _[Total War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total\_War\_(video\_game\_series) "Total War (video game series)")_ series, the game was released for [Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows "Windows") on May 23, 2019. [Feral Interactive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feral_Interactive "Feral Interactive") released a [Linux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linux "Linux") and [macOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacOS "MacOS") version of the game on the same day.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-1)

## Gameplay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Gameplay")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/d/d4/Total_War_Three_Kingdoms_screenshot.jpg/250px-Total_War_Three_Kingdoms_screenshot.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Total_War_Three_Kingdoms_screenshot.jpg)

In _Total War: Three Kingdoms_, generals can engage in a one-versus-one [dueling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dueling "Dueling"), which ends when one of them dies or flees.

Like its predecessors, _Total War: Three Kingdoms_ is a [turn-based strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn-based_strategy "Turn-based strategy")[real-time tactics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real-time_tactics "Real-time tactics") game. Set during the [End of the Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_the_Han_dynasty "End of the Han dynasty") (189-220) and into the [Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Kingdoms "Three Kingdoms") era (220–280), the player controls one of the factions, who must eliminate or vassalize other factions, gaining enough prestige to declare themselves Emperor. The player must also defeat the other two Emperors which are the two most powerful factions, unify [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") and become its ultimate ruler.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-2) These factions are led by warlords, such as [Cao Cao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cao_Cao "Cao Cao"), [Liu Bei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Bei "Liu Bei"), and [Sun Quan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Quan "Sun Quan").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-3) In siege battles, the player commands both infantry and cavalry units. All the units featured in the game are divided into different [retinues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retinue "Retinue"), with each led by a powerful general. The player can deploy up to three generals into the battlefield at once along with three in reserve, and there will only be access to the units that those generals can recruit.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-4)

The player wins a siege battle when all hostile generals are killed or the central point of the city is captured. These generals, which can be commanded separately from their troops, have the possession of unique ancillaries, that can be looted once they are killed. For instance, [Lü Bu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%BC_Bu "Lü Bu")'s [Red Hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hare "Red Hare") can be captured and used by other generals. Generals can engage in a one-versus-one [dueling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dueling "Dueling"), which ends when one of them dies or flees. Each general has different classes and specialties, granting their units with both active and passive buffs.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-5) The team introduces the concept of "[guanxi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanxi "Guanxi")" to the game, in which each general will form social connections and relationships with other characters. Viewing concepts like "obligations, reciprocity, and trust" as important virtues, these generals have unique personalities and desires that the player needs to cater to. If their demands are not met, their happiness rating will drop and this may lead to various repercussions.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-guanxi-6) Unlike previous _Total War_ games where characters rarely interact with each other, the generals featured in the game are actively forming relationships with the people they meet throughout the campaign. This adds a strategic layer to the game in which players need to understand these generals before making any decisions.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-guanxi-6)

The game features two modes. The first mode, "Romance", is based on the novel _[Romance of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance\_of\_the\_Three\_Kingdoms "Romance of the Three Kingdoms")_, in which generals are gifted with nearly superhuman strength. Another mode, "Records", based on _[Records of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Records\_of\_the\_Three\_Kingdoms "Records of the Three Kingdoms")_, presents a more historically authentic version. In Records, the generals have their powers removed and they can no longer be commanded separately, in addition to changing certain equipment in-game to be more historically authentic.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-7)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Plot")]

Taking place in 190 AD, the once glorious [Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") is on the verge of collapse. The new emperor, [Emperor Xian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_Xian_of_Han "Emperor Xian of Han"), enthroned at the age of eight, was manipulated by the warlord [Dong Zhuo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dong_Zhuo "Dong Zhuo"), whose oppressive rule leads to chaos. New warlords rise and form alliances to start the [campaign against Dong Zhuo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_against_Dong_Zhuo "Campaign against Dong Zhuo"). With each warlord having personal ambitions and allegiances constantly shifting, the champions that emerge from the everlasting wars will shape the future of China.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-premise-8)

## Development and release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Development and release")]

The game was developed by [Creative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Assembly "Creative Assembly"). Creative Assembly had refined many elements of the game, bringing changes to both the [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") and the [user interface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User_interface "User interface"). The team introduced the system of "guanxi" in order to make the characters and generals more important in the game, as _Records_ and _Romances_, two of the team's most prominent source materials, have a huge focus on characters. The [sinologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinology "Sinology")[Rafe de Crespigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafe_de_Crespigny "Rafe de Crespigny"), an expert on the era, acted as a consultant for the game.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-9)

When the game was still in preproduction in November 2016, Creative Assembly announced that the next historical _Total War_ title would explore a new era instead of being a sequel to any prior game.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-10)_Three Kingdoms_ was revealed by publisher [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega") on January 11, 2018 with a cinematic trailer.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-premise-8) Originally set to be released in the second half of 2018, the game was delayed to early 2019 so that the team had additional development time to complete the production.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-11) A new release date of March 7, 2019 was later announced, which was then delayed to May 23, 2019.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-13)

_Total War: Three Kingdoms_ received positive reviews from critics, with many specifically praising the character-driven gameplay mechanics and storytelling elements. Chris Wray of wccftech describes the game is "as close to flawless, with a fantastic balance of [4X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4X "4X") strategy and character-focused development and emergent storytelling."[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-30)_[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")_'s TJ Hafer stated that _Three Kingdoms_ should serve as the example for all games of its genre going forward.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-ignreview-23) Edwin Evans-Thirlwell of _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ stated the game "...is a wonderfully torrid period epic that understands the greatest stories are written about people, not empires."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-Guardian-26) Jody Macgregor of _[PC Gamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PC\_Gamer "PC Gamer")_ praised the campaign elements, but found the game still could not break off from longstanding problems the series has always faced, claiming _Three Kingdoms_ "is not the best Total War game but not the worst by a long shot."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-PCGUS-24)

The Romance mode has also been praised as bringing fascinating additions to the game, with many reviewers comparing it to _[Total War: Warhammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total\_War:\_Warhammer "Total War: Warhammer")_. Preston Dozsa of _CGMagazine_ stated that the game "represents the best of both the historical and fantasy sides of the franchise."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-31) Sean Martin from Hooked Gamers stated the game "is the most divergent _Total War_ I’ve seen since _Total War: Warhammer._.. taking what is good in fantasy and using it to complement the historical components of the game."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-32) Denis Ryan of _[Rock, Paper, Shotgun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock,\_Paper,\_Shotgun "Rock, Paper, Shotgun")_ said it draws inspiration from many games that [Creative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Assembly "Creative Assembly") developed in the past, and "despite the resemblance there really is no game which has quite the same combination of elements, nor is there any strategy game that looks this good."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-RPS-28)

Chris Tapsell of _[Eurogamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurogamer "Eurogamer")_ also stated that the game is "ambitious and sometimes overwhelming."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-EuroG-20)_[PCGamesN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PCGamesN "PCGamesN")_'s Phil Iwaniuk said the game brings issues along with innovations, and noted that despite the memorable campaign, the real-time battles portion lacks depth compared to rest of the series.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-PCGN-25)

Beifang Lin of _GamerSky_, a Chinese publication, commended the development team for their professionalism and deep understanding of the historical era, concluding that the Three Kingdoms theme was well integrated into the _Total War_ system.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-gskyreview-27)

### Sales

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Sales")]

According to the developer Creative Assembly, _Total War: Three Kingdoms_ was the most pre-ordered _[Total War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total\_War\_(video\_game\_series) "Total War (video game series)")_ game until its release date.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-PCGN_sale-33) The game also set the record of concurrent players for _Total War_ series, with over 160,000 people playing simultaneously on the day of release and reaching 192,000 by the first weekend. This made it the largest concurrent played strategy game on Steam.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-Pcgamer_sale-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-37) It became the fastest-selling game in the history of the franchise, selling one million copies in a week since its initial release[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-38) and amassed a total of 3,210,000 units sold as of March 2025.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_War:_Three_Kingdoms#cite_note-39)
